name: Wisconsin

notes: Food for home consumption is exempt; candy, soft drinks, dietary supplements and prepared food are taxed at the full rate, which is not counted here.

Cigarettes and other tobacco are taxed at the full rate, on top of excise taxes left out here: $2.52 a pack of cigarettes, 71% of the manufacturer's list price on other tobacco, and 5 cents a milliliter of vapor liquid.
Barber and beauty services aren't taxed.
Laundry, dry cleaning, pressing and dyeing are taxed; self-service coin-operated machines are not (since October 1, 2013).
Motor fuel is exempt from the sales tax and taxed by the gallon instead: 30.9 cents, unchanged since April 1, 2006, left out here.
Diapers and menstrual products are taxed at the full rate (2025 bills to exempt them stayed in committee, as reported).
Wisconsin has no sales tax holiday.

Hotel stays pay municipal room taxes (generally up to 8%; Madison 10%, Wisconsin Dells 5.5% plus its resort tax) and, in Milwaukee County, the Wisconsin Center District's room taxes, which are not counted here.
gaps: 6 cities lie in more than one county with a different rate in each county part; a tract at least half in such a city takes the rate of its own county part.
1241 towns or townships that are not Census places have their rates listed here, matched to tracts through Census county subdivisions; all carry only the county rate.

Premier resort area taxes (10 places; 1.25% in Lake Delton and Wisconsin Dells, 0.5% in the others) and Milwaukee County's 0.5% food and beverage tax are administered outside the SST rate file; they are counted in the categories they fall on, as each place's notes say.

5505350: Bayfield's 0.5% premier resort area tax (since January 1, 2003; Department of Revenue) is added to the taxable sales of restaurants, bars, apparel, drug, liquor, general merchandise, gift, sporting goods and toy shops and lodging and amusements, not grocery stores; it would be counted in the rates for restaurants, drinks served and apparel here, and for alcohol bought in stores in the share sold where it applies (about 59% of those sales nationally, 2022 Economic Census), not in the others.
Bayfield is less than half of each census tract it is in, so the figures here use the surrounding area's rates for its tract, not its own.

The district's 3% room tax (10% in all in Milwaukee) and 3% car rental tax are not counted (Department of Revenue).

programs: Tax incremental districts are mapped from city and county layers; any the Department of Revenue lists as ended (its termination reports for 2023 to 2026, or a number below a municipality's highest active district that isn't on its April 2026 active list) is left out, since several maps still draw ended districts (Milwaukee's, Madison's, Adams's, De Pere's and others). Madison's TID 55 (Voit Farm, 2025), Green Bay's newer districts (24 to 32) and Sun Prairie's TID 16 aren't on their maps. Business improvement districts are mapped for Milwaukee and Fond du Lac; Madison's Central BID and the Stevens Point and Sun Prairie districts have no official map. Enterprise zones are designated per company, and Main Street (36) and Connect Communities (94) have no map.

warn: Wisconsin Dells lies in four counties; the figures here are for the Columbia County tract that holds most of it, not its Sauk County part.

warn.text: Rhinelander draws many visitors (it levies a premier resort area tax), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy: its seasonal homes (5.2%) and its 10 lodging places (1.1 per 1,000 residents) fall under the flag's cutoffs. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

Baraboo draws many visitors (Devil's Lake and the Dells nearby), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy: its seasonal homes (1.8%) and its 15 lodging places (1.1 per 1,000 residents) fall under the flag's cutoffs. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

Sauk County draws many visitors (Lake Delton and part of Wisconsin Dells), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy: its seasonal homes (6.5%) fall under the cutoff and its 142 lodging places (2.15 per 1,000 residents) just under it (2.17), though 6 of its 24 census tracts are flagged on their own. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.
